clinicalPearls: It is essential to distinguish physiological gastro-oesophageal reflux, which is common and benign in healthy infants, from reflux disease, in which reflux causes troublesome symptoms or complications.
Effortless regurgitation or posseting in a thriving, comfortable infant (the happy spitter) is normal and typically improves as the infant matures and begins to sit and take solids.
Reflux disease is suggested by poor weight gain, feeding refusal or distress, persistent irritability, back-arching with feeds, or respiratory symptoms attributable to reflux.
Diagnosis is largely clinical from the history and examination; investigations are reserved for atypical presentations, complications, or diagnostic uncertainty.
First-line management uses conservative measures such as optimising feeding volume and technique, thickened feeds where appropriate, and positioning advice consistent with safe sleep guidance.
A trial of cow's milk protein elimination is reasonable when allergy is suspected, since it can mimic or coexist with reflux disease.
Acid-suppressing medication is not appropriate for uncomplicated physiological reflux and should be limited to infants with clear evidence of reflux disease.
Warning features such as bilious or forceful vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, or onset of vomiting after six months point away from simple reflux and toward an alternative diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Gastro-oesophageal reflux occurs when gastric contents pass back into the oesophagus, largely through transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter. Reflux is especially common in infancy because of a short oesophagus, a predominantly liquid and high-volume diet, frequent recumbency, and immaturity of the antireflux barrier. In most infants this is physiological and self-resolving. Reflux disease develops when refluxate causes oesophageal mucosal injury and pain, impairs feeding and growth, or reaches the airway to provoke respiratory symptoms. Contributing factors include delayed gastric emptying and, in some infants, cow's milk protein allergy that produces overlapping symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Intestinal obstruction or malrotation (particularly with bilious vomiting)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment with growth monitoring (usually sufficient)
Trial of cow's milk protein elimination when allergy is suspected
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study to assess anatomy if obstruction or malrotation is a concern
Oesophageal pH or impedance monitoring in selected complex cases
Endoscopy when oesophagitis or another mucosal complication is suspected
redFlags: Forceful or projectile vomiting suggesting pyloric stenosis
Onset of vomiting after six months or persistence beyond infancy
Systemic signs such as fever, lethargy, or a bulging fontanelle
reference.prognosis: Physiological reflux resolves in the great majority of infants during the first year to eighteen months as the infant matures; reflux disease also generally improves with time and appropriate management, though some infants with underlying conditions require more prolonged treatment.
pitfalls: Treating benign physiological reflux with acid suppression or unnecessary investigation
Missing an alternative diagnosis such as pyloric stenosis or malrotation presenting with vomiting
Overlooking cow's milk protein allergy as a mimicking or coexisting cause
Recommending positioning that conflicts with safe sleep advice
management: Reassurance and conservative measures for physiological reflux in a thriving infant, including feed-volume and technique optimisation, thickened feeds and positioning consistent with safe-sleep advice
A trial of cow's milk protein elimination, using maternal dairy exclusion in breastfed infants or an extensively hydrolysed formula, where allergy is suspected
Acid suppression with a proton pump inhibitor or H2-receptor antagonist reserved for proven reflux disease or oesophagitis, not for uncomplicated regurgitation
Avoidance of routine acid-suppressing medication for effortless regurgitation alone
Growth monitoring and feeding support to detect faltering growth and feeding difficulty
Referral for paediatric specialist assessment and investigation for atypical features, complications or treatment failure, with fundoplication reserved for severe refractory disease
